description:
RAID (originally redundant array of inexpensive disks, now commonly redundant array of independent disks) allows information to be spread across several disks. RAID uses techniques such as
disk striping (RAID Level 0)
disk mirroring (RAID Level 1)
and disk striping with parity (RAID Level 5)
to achieve redundancy, lower latency, increased bandwidth, and maximized ability to recover from hard disk crashes.

RAID distributes data across each drive in the array by breaking it down into consistently-sized chunks (commonly 256K or 512k, although other values are acceptable). Each chunk is then written to a hard drive in the RAID array according to the RAID level employed. When the data is read, the process is reversed, giving the illusion that the multiple drives in the array are actually one large drive.

RAID supports various configurations, including levels 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 10, and linear. These RAID 0 and 1 types are defined as follows: For other types of RAID, please check read Wiki

Level 0
RAID level 0, often called striping is a performance-oriented striped data mapping technique. This means the data being written to the array is broken down into strips and written across the member disks of the array, allowing high I/O performance at low inherent cost but provides no redundancy.

Level 1
RAID level 1, or mirroring, has been used longer than any other form of RAID. Level 1 provides redundancy by writing identical data to each member disk of the array, leaving a mirrored copy on each disk. Mirroring remains popular due to its simplicity and high level of data availability. Level 1 operates with two or more disks, and provides very good data reliability and improves performance for read-intensive applications but at a relatively high cost.
name: What is Software RAID?

description:
Setting up RAID volumes requires the mdadm package; it provides the mdadm command, which allows creating and manipulating RAID arrays, as well as scripts and tools integrating it to the rest of the system, including the monitoring system.So Install the command first on your distro

yum -y install mdadm wget
We need setup some partition on our drives. So run these two commands

url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakshmipathi/scripts/master/fdisk.sh"
wget $url -O - | bash
to create them.
Now, Our example will be a server with a number of disks, some of which are already used, the rest being available to setup RAID. We initially have the following disks and partitions:
  • the xvdb disk, 6 GB, partitions xvdb5,xvdb6,xvdb7 (about 2 GB each) are available
  • the xvdc disk, 4 GB, xvdc5,xvdc6 (about 2GB each are available)
You can view this setup using command like
fdisk -l
The /proc/mdstat file lists existing volumes and their states. When creating a new RAID volume, care should be taken not to name it the same as an existing volume. We're going to use these physical elements to build two volumes, one RAID-0 and one mirror (RAID-1).
name: Setting up RAID

answer: RAID-0 is also known as "Stripping" and 512KB is the Chunk Size (see --detail output).
description:
Let's start with setting up RAID-0,we will use /dev/xvdc5 and /dev/xvdb5 each has 2GB disk space.Note that we carefully chosen partition from different drives. So that If drives we can use the data from other drive,which is true for RAID-1.

mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=0 --raid-devices=2 /dev/xvdc5 /dev/xvdb5 
mdadm: Defaulting to version 1.2 metadata
mdadm: array /dev/md0 started.
The mdadm --create command requires several parameters: the name of the volume to create (/dev/md*, with MD standing for Multiple Device), the RAID level, the number of disks (which is compulsory despite being mostly meaningful only with RAID-1 and above), and the physical drives to use. Once the device is created, we can use it like we'd use a normal partition, create a filesystem on it, mount that filesystem, and so on. Note that our creation of a RAID-0 volume on md0 is nothing but coincidence, and the numbering of the array doesn't need to be correlated to the chosen amount of redundancy. It's also possible to create named RAID arrays, by giving mdadm parameters such as /dev/md/linearinstead of /dev/md0.
We can check the details of newly created RAID 0 with -query or -detail commands or do cat /proc/mdstat
mdadm --query /dev/md0 
/dev/md0: 4.01GiB raid0 2 devices, 0 spares. Use mdadm --detail for more detail.

And for detailed info about RAID0 and its drives
mdadm --detail /dev/md0

lets format the raid-device /dev/md0
mkfs.ext3 /dev/md0 
mke2fs 1.41.12 (17-May-2010)
Filesystem label=
OS type: Linux
Block size=4096 (log=2)
...

mount the drive
mkdir /srv/raid-0
# mount /dev/md0 /srv/raid-0
# df -h /srv/raid-0
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/md0        4.0G  137M  3.7G   4% /srv/raid-0

Now you can create some files on /src/raid-0. Content of file will be stored on both xvdb5 and /xvdc5. To visualize RAID-0,assume if you have content hello then 
byte h will go to xvdb5 , byte e will go to xvdc6
byte l will go to xvdb5 , byte l will go to xvdc6
byte o will go to xvdb5
Here we said, each byte will go to a drive, but in reality this size is known as chunk size
To stop RAID0, just perform
mdadm --stop /dev/md0 
mdadm: stopped /dev/md0
and to restart
mdadm --assemble --scan

What's another name for RAID-0 and Whats the Chunk size for /dev/md0 ?

description:
Creation of a RAID-1 follows a similar fashion, the differences only being noticeable after the creation:
mdadm --create /dev/md1 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/xvdc6 /dev/xvdb6
Again you know the three ways to check the details either from /proc/mdstat or using --query or --detail commands. right?

Now go ahead and format RAID-1 /dev/md1 and mount it. This part is similar to previous session.

Lets visualize RAID-1,assume if you have content hello in file.txt then 
entire content hello will go to xvdc6
and another copy  hello will go to xvdb6


Yes, with RAID-1, we have a exact copy on both drives. So that you can have access to data even if drives goes down. Downside is, it consumes twice the file size. Do you know what's RAID-1 is called?
name: Setup RAID-1

description:
Now let's see what happens when one of the elements of the RAID-1 array fails. mdadm, in particular its --fail option, allows simulating such a disk failure:

mdadm /dev/md1 --fail /dev/xvdb6 
 mdadm: set /dev/xvdb6 faulty in /dev/md1

now check the status using /proc/mdstat and notice the difference? Its noted as F Faulty. Even the --detail agree with this output.
mdadm --detail /dev/md1
The contents of the volume are still accessible (and, if it is mounted, the applications don't notice a thing), but the data safety isn't assured anymore: should the xvdc disk fail in turn, the data would be lost. We want to avoid that risk, so we'll replace the failed disk with a new one, We will see that in next section.
name: Drive failure with RAID-1

description:
Lets add a new drive xvdb7 and remove this drive xvdb6
Add a new drive
mdadm /dev/md1 --add /dev/xvdb7 
mdadm: added /dev/xvdb7

Here again, the kernel automatically triggers a reconstruction phase during which the volume, although still accessible, is in a degraded mode. Once the reconstruction is over, the RAID array is back to a normal state. One can then tell the system that the xvdb disk is about to be removed from the array, so as to end up with a classical RAID mirror on two disks:
mdadm /dev/md1 --remove /dev/xvdb6 
 mdadm: hot removed /dev/xvdb6 from /dev/md1

You can monitor the sync process using cat /proc/mdstat 
Personalities : [raid0] [raid1]
